Surah Al-Ma'un

It is also called "Surat Ara'ayta," and "Al-Din" and "Al-Takdhib." It is Meccan according to the majority; Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, as cited in al-Durr al-Manthur. In al-Bahr it is said that it is Medinan according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, and this is also reported from al-Dahhak. Hibat Allah, the blind exegete, said: half of it was revealed in Mecca concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il, and half in Medina concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, the hypocrite. Its verses are seven according to the Iraqi reckoning and six according to the others.

When the Exalted, in Surat Quraysh, mentioned: ﴿He who fed them against hunger﴾, He, Mighty and Majestic, here censured those who did not urge the feeding of the needy. When He, may He be exalted, said there: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾, He censured here those who are heedless of their prayer. Or, when He enumerated His blessings upon Quraysh, and they did not believe in resurrection and recompense, the Exalted followed His favour upon them with a threat of recompense and a warning of His punishment. So the Mighty One said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Din?﴾ This is an interrogative intended to arouse the listener's eagerness to know the denier, and that this is something the religious person must know in order to guard against him and his deeds. It also includes a note of wonder at him. The address is to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or to everyone who is fit for it. "Ra'ayta" (seeing) here means knowing, which takes one object. Al-Hufi said: it may be visual (basariyyah), and on both readings it may be used figuratively for informing, so that the meaning of "ara'ayta" is "inform me," and then it takes two objects: the first being the relative pronoun, and the second being omitted, its estimate being "who is he? Is he not deserving of punishment?" The claim that the figurative sense of seeing is only ever visual and cannot take the particle of address is open to question; likewise the blanket statement that the particle of address does not attach to the visual sense is not decisive, since there is no barrier to it after the figurative extension. Therefore it is not preferred that it be cognitive. The reading of 'Abd Allah: «Ara'aytuka» with the added particle of address (kaf al-khitab) for emphasis of the ta'.

"Al-Din" means recompense (al-jaza'), which is one of its meanings, and from it comes the saying: "As you do, so shall be done to you." Mujahid's statement regarding its meaning is: reckoning or Islam, as is most well known; and perhaps this is what those who explained it as the Qur'an intended. Likewise those who explained it, like Ibn 'Abbas, as the judgment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Kisa'i read «Ara'yta» with the hamza omitted, as if he analogized the past tense in omitting its hamza to its present tense, where omission is regular. This is like "ta'idu" being assimilated to "ya'idu" in the rules of weak letters. Perhaps the initial placement of the hamza of interrogation before the verb here eased the omission in it, due to its resemblance to the present-tense form beginning with a hamza. For this reason this reading is stronger in its justification than what occurs in the line of verse:

"O companion, have you seen (rayta) or heard of a shepherd who returned into the udder what he had gathered in the milk-pails?"

It has also been said that after the interrogative hamza, "ara" (the past of seeing) was attached in the manner of verbs, because of its strong resemblance to it, and there is no difference except a fatha, which because of its lightness is treated as sukun. But this is not the case, even though it is claimed to be the more likely view.

The fa' in His words, ﴿Then that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾, has been said to be for causation (al-sababiyyah, indicating cause), so that what follows is the effect of the arousal of interest (al-tashwiq) implied by the preceding discourse. It has also been said that it falls in the answer to an omitted conditional (shart mahdhuf, an understood "if" clause), with dhalika being the subject (mubtada') and the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: "Have you come to know the one who denies the Recompense or Islam? If you do not know him, then that one who denies it, that is the one who repulses the orphan," that is, he pushes him away forcefully and drives him off with a harsh rebuff. The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) has been placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate contempt. It has also been said that it is to indicate the cause of the ruling. Moreover, the use of the relative pronoun indicates the certainty of the relation (al-silah), which is not hidden.

Ali, may God honor his face, and al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and al-Yamani read «yada'" (yadaʿu) with a light pronunciation (al-takhfif), meaning: he leaves the orphan, does not show him kindness, and treats him with harshness.

﴿And does not urge﴾ means: and does not incite anyone from his own family or others among the wealthy ﴿to feed the poor﴾, that is, to give away food for the needy, meaning what is consumed as sustenance. The expression "food" (ṭaʿām) is used rather than "feeding" (iṭʿām), even though it requires the implied noun (muḍāf) to be supplied, as we have pointed out, to indicate that the needy person is as if he were the owner of what is given to him, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾. This indicates the intensity of his entitlement. There is also in it an allusion to the prohibition of reproaching the recipient with benefaction. It has been said: the word "ṭaʿām" here means "iṭʿām" (feeding), and the statement of al-Rāghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) allows for this, so no implied noun is needed. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read «لا يحاضّ» (lā yuḥāḍḍu), the present tense of ḥāḍaḍtu. This clause is coordinated with the relative clause and falls together with it within the scope of the definition of the one who denies (the religion). Thus, Glorified and Exalted is He, has made his sign the readiness to harm the weak and the failure to give kindness, in the sense that this is part of his nature and the necessary consequences of his kind.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 107, verses 4–5:**

﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾. That is: they are negligent and unconcerned about it, to the point that it completely escapes them, or its time passes, or they do not perform it as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the early generations (*al-salaf*, the first three generations of Muslims) performed it. Rather, they peck at it (*naqr*, performing it hastily, like a bird pecking), they do not humble themselves in it, they "rush" (*yunjidun*) and "go astray" (*yutbihun*) in it, and they wander (*yahimun*) in every valley of thoughts that are unsuitable to it. So one of them finishes the prayer without knowing what he recited in it, and so on, of other things that indicate little concern for it.

The early scholars have many statements about the meaning of this heedlessness, and perhaps all of them are a matter of illustration (*tamthil*, giving examples of a general meaning). From Abu al-Aliyah: it is turning away to the right and the left. From Qatadah: a person's lack of concern whether he prayed or did not pray. From Ibn Abbas and a group: delaying it beyond its time. There is a hadith about this which many have narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), but al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi said: its being a statement of Sa'd (*mawquf*) is more authentic. From Abu al-Aliyah also: it is that a person does not know how many units (*raka'at*) he has completed, whether an even number (*shaf'*) or an odd number (*witr*).

Some scholars interpreted heedlessness of the prayer as abandoning it, and said: the meaning of "those who pray" is those who are marked with the mark of the people of prayer, if by "abandonment" is meant total abandonment and complete non-performance; or those who pray in general, if by "abandonment" is meant abandoning it at times.

﴿Those who make a show [of their deeds]﴾ before people, performing them where people can see them, and seeking praise from them.

[Ruh al-Ma'ani, Commentary of al-Alusi, on surah 107, verse 7]

﴿And they withhold the ma'un (small kindnesses)﴾: that is, the zakat (obligatory alms), as was reported from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, and from his son Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Dahhak and ʿIkrima. From this is the verse of al-Raʿi:

O Caliph of the Merciful, we are a company of hanifs (upright monotheists), prostrating morning and evening.
Arabs who see in our wealth for God the due of zakat, sent down as a sending down.
A people who, upon Islam, have not withheld their ma'un nor neglected the tahlil (the declaration "There is no god but God").

And from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Kalbi: it is all that is good (al-maʿruf kulluhu). A group reported from Ibn Masʿud an explanation of it as what people lend to one another among themselves, such as the cooking pot, the bucket, the axe and similar household goods. This is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas in a report transmitted from him by al-Diya' in [his book] al-Mukhtara, by al-Hakim, who authenticated it, by al-Bayhaqi and others, and they transmitted from him several marfuʿ (traced back to the Prophet) hadiths on this. Withholding that may be forbidden in the Sharia, as when it is requested out of necessity, and disgraceful in terms of manliness (muruwwa), as when it is requested when there is no necessity. And it is, according to what Ibn Abi Shayba reported from al-Zuhri, "mal" (property) in the language of Quraysh.

Abu ʿUbayda, al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said: it refers, in the Jahiliyya, to everything that has benefit, whether little or much, and by it is meant in Islam obedience. Its root has been disputed. Qutrub said: its root is fa'ul from al-maʿn, which is a little thing, and they said: "ma lahu maʿanat," meaning, "he has a little thing." It was also said: its root is maʿuna, and the alif is a substitute for the ha', so its form originally is mafʿal, like makram, so the mim is an added letter; and its form after the addition of the alif as a substitute is "ma faʿala."

It was also said: it is an ism maf'ul (passive participle) from aʿana yuʿinu, and its root is maʿun; it was transposed so that its ʿayn took the place of its fa', becoming mawʿun, then the waw was changed into an alif, becoming maʿun, a maf'ul with the ʿayn placed before the fa'.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So woe﴾ etc., is a consequential fa' (linking to a result), and the speech is an ascent from that known description to a stronger known description. That is: if pushing away the orphan and urging the feeding of the poor are in this station, then what of the worshipper who is heedless of his prayer, which is the pillar of religion and the distinguisher between belief and disbelief, who commits showing-off (riya') in his deeds, which is a branch of shirk, and who withholds zakat, which is the twin of prayer and the bridge of Islam, or who withholds lending a thing, which people customarily lend, let alone paying zakat from his property? That is the mark of denial which is not hidden, and the known description that is not fulfilled. The purpose is to intensify the condemnation of these vices with which many people are afflicted, and that since they are among the marks of one who denies the religion, it is incumbent upon the believer who holds it to keep far from them by long distances, and to realize that the mother of every disobedience is denial of the religion. The intended "denier" in this case is the genus, and the demonstrative does not prevent that, as is not hidden.

It was also said: he is Abu Jahl, who was the guardian of an orphan, and the orphan came to him naked, asking him from his own property, and he pushed him with a shameful push. Ibn Jurayj said: he is Abu Sufyan, who slaughtered a camel, and an orphan asked him for meat, so he struck him with his staff. It was also said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; it was also said: al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il; it was also said: ʿAmr ibn ʿAʾidh; it was also said: a stingy hypocrite. On all these sayings the one referred to is specific, and then the view that those heedless of prayer and showing-off are also specific holds.

The author of al-Kashf said: "It is not suitable; rather it is a kind of digression derived from the known description, meaning pushing the orphan. The sense is that if pushing is, in its state, the mark of the denier, then what is the state of heedlessness in prayer and what is joined to it, which are more and more severe?" It was made a kind of digression, as he said, because the speech is about denial, not about warning against pushing as a primary matter; and the intended genus is true with the plural. And that this is an evident strain, as some have said, is not evident. It is as if it were said: Tell me what you say about those who deny the religion and those who push the orphan: is their state good and their doing, or ugly?

The purpose is to affirm the judgment of ugliness in the manner of His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ Then it was said: "So woe to the worshippers," meaning: when it is known that their state is ugly, then woe to them. He placed "the worshippers" in place of the pronoun, indicating that together with being described by denial, they are also described by these things.

Some of them made the fa' in "So woe" a causal fa' according to the said conjunction, and this view requires the identity of the worshippers and the deniers; and on this it was said: the intended by them are the hypocrites. Rather, the statement that they are the intended is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Imam Malik.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "It is indicated by ﴿Those who show off﴾. It is possible that the worshippers be intended in the general sense: those charged with prayer, even if they are unbelievers, not hypocrites, and their heedlessness of prayer means their abandoning it entirely; and it is required to hold that unbelievers are charged with the subsidiary laws absolutely."

Abu Hayyan objected to that view that the construction according to it is a strange construction, like your saying: "I honored the one who visits me, so that is the one who does good to me." What comes to mind from it is that "dhalika" is nominative by the beginning, and on the supposition of accusative by conjunction the sense would be: "I honored the one who visits me, so I honored that one who does good to me." The demonstrative in it is not fully used as the eloquent usage would have it, since there is no need for it; rather the eloquent would be: "I honored the one who visits me, so the one who does good to me," or "I honored the one who visits me, so he does good to me." It was said: the demonstrative here is inserted to indicate the distance of his rank in evil and corruption. So consider.

It is also permitted that the conjunction be a conjunction of essence to essence, so the inquiry about the state of the deniers and the state of those who push is: is it good or ugly, on the analogy of what has passed.

The author of al-Kashf objected to this, saying that it does not suit the context for the pronoun to refer to the two groups, so that "the worshippers" is placed in its place. So understand.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Ashhab read: "yaruʾuna," with qasr (short vowel) and shadda on the hamza. In another transmission from Ibn Ishaq, he read with qasr and without shadda. And God knows best.
